reading.title: How Newcomers Reshape a Neighborhood
reading.purpose: Explore how communities balance shared civic life with family heritage and belonging.
paras: Walk down a busy street in almost any large port city and you can taste, hear, and read a living story of arrival. Bakery signs sit beside tailor shops and halls. Each shop reflects the ancestry—the family lines and earlier generations—of the people who built the block. For newcomers, building a shared life without losing their own identity is a lifelong test.

In past eras, many cities pushed immigrants to assimilate fully, asking them to adopt new habits and drop old languages at the door. Younger people often felt urged to conform to local styles so they would not stand out at school or work. When schools or bosses marginalize a group—treating its voices as small and pushing them to the edges—people feel cut off. Harsh teasing or unfair rules can soon alienate newcomers, making them feel like outsiders in the town they help build.

Yet towns also show a wiser path. Instead of asking for sameness, strong towns work to integrate groups so all share schools, parks, and halls as equal partners. Aid clubs, street fairs, and local choirs build solidarity, a deep sense of unity and support among people working toward shared goals.

Inside that wide story lives a quiet personal one. A student may wear a breezy public persona at school, showing a bold outer image while feeling far more introspective at home, quietly thinking over family memories and hopes. Cities grow richest when people do not have to erase their roots just to belong where they live.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "persona" most nearly means
choices: the family line of grandparents and earlier relatives
the public outer image a person shows to other people
the shared street festival that unites a neighborhood
the official set of rules taught inside a port city school
qs.why: Paragraph 4 restates persona directly as "projecting a confident outer image" in contrast to private thoughts at home.

qs.q: Which sentence gives specific examples of activities that build unity across a neighborhood?
choices: Yet towns also show a wiser path.
Instead of asking for sameness, strong towns work to integrate groups so all share schools, parks, and halls as equal partners.
Aid clubs, street fairs, and local choirs build solidarity, a deep sense of unity and support among people working toward shared goals.
Cities grow richest when people do not have to erase their roots just to belong where they live.
qs.why: This sentence lists three concrete community activities—aid clubs, street fairs, and local choirs—that create solidarity.

ev.text: Aid clubs, street fairs, and local choirs build solidarity, a deep sense of unity and support among people working toward shared goals.

qs.q: How does the reading contrast assimilating with integrating?
choices: Assimilating pressures newcomers to drop old traditions, while integrating welcomes equal participation.
Assimilating happens only in small towns, while integrating happens only near busy port bakeries.
Assimilating helps people keep their ancestry, while integrating asks students to hide their feelings.
Assimilating is led by neighborhood choirs, while integrating is required by strict city laws.
qs.why: Paragraph 2 links assimilating to dropping old languages and habits, whereas paragraph 3 says integrating brings groups together as equal partners without demanding sameness.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Port cities are the only places where bakeries and tailor shops stay open for generations.
Communities thrive best when newcomers can share civic life without erasing their heritage.
Students who act confident at school are rarely quiet or thoughtful when they return home.
Unfair teasing in schools can only be solved by ending all neighborhood street festivals.
qs.why: The reading contrasts pressure to conform and marginalization with integration and solidarity, concluding that belonging should not require erasing heritage.
